claim_1.claim: Bulk RNA-seq assay analysis of platelet-rich plasma from 28 young adults, 20 community-dwelling older adults, and 17 skilled nursing facility-resident older adults before vaccination (day 0) showed platelet activation pathways, Rho GTPase effector pathways, and mitochondrial genes were increased in Older (Comm) versus Young adults, with platelet activation pathways further increased in Older (SNF) versus Older (Comm), while translation-related pathways decreased across these age/frailty groups.

sources.quote: This analysis found 1508 RNAs that were significantly different when comparing Young to Older (Comm) adults, and 2209 RNAs that were significantly different when comparing Older (Comm) to Older (SNF) adults (|log2fc| >1.5, adj. p value <0.05, Table 2 ). Platelet activation pathways were significantly enriched in Older (Comm) compared with young adults, as were Rho GTPase effector pathways mediating the activation response (Aslan & McCarty, 2013 ) and mitochondrial genes (Table 2 , Extended Data Figure S2b ). Notably, activation pathways in platelets from Older (SNF) adults were also significantly increased compared to Older (Comm) adults.

In contrast to the age‐associated increase in platelet activation RNAs, RNAs in pathways related to translation decreased with age and SNF resident status. These pathways were enriched in Young compared to Older (Comm) and Older (Comm) compared to Older (SNF) adults (Table 2 , Tables S1–S4 ).

We enrolled 28 young adults (age 21–35 years), 20 community‐dwelling older adults (age ≥65 years) (Older (Comm)), and 17 older adults (age ≥65 years) (Older (SNF)) who were residents of a skilled nursing facility (SNF) in greater New Haven, Connecticut (Table 1 ).
Blood samples were collected prior to vaccination (day 0) and follow‐up days 2, 7, and 28.

claim_2.claim: Bulk RNA-seq assay analysis of platelet-rich plasma from participants with complete longitudinal data at baseline before vaccination (day 0) and days 2, 7, and 28 after vaccination (day 2, day 7, and day 28) showed distinct age-group trajectories of platelet activation RNAs: Component 1 increased and remained stable in young adults, Component 2 showed a sustained post-vaccination decrease in Older (SNF) adults, and Component 5 showed a drop then return to baseline in Older (Comm) adults.

sources.quote: Component 1 was associated with young adults, and represents a temporal expression pattern where RNA expression increased post‐vaccination and remained stable. In Component 2, which was associated with Older (SNF) adults, pre‐vaccination RNA levels experienced a sustained drop post‐vaccination and in Component 5, associated with Older (Comm) adults, pre‐vaccination RNA levels experienced a drop followed by a rise back to pre‐vaccination levels.
Pathways involving platelet degranulation, platelet activation, and hemostasis were significantly over‐represented (platelet activation genes PF4 and PPBP were members of this intersecting set).
Blood samples were collected prior to vaccination (day 0) and follow‐up days 2, 7, and 28.
Only participants with data for all days in the study were used. The final dimensions of the tensor were 500 × 54 × 4.

claim_3.claim: Bulk RNA-seq assay analysis of platelet-rich plasma from young adults showed that high versus low vaccine responders differed in post-vaccination platelet activation RNA trajectories, with Component 2 RNAs including PF4 and PPBP decreasing on days 7-28 after vaccination (day 7-day 28) in high responders (n = 7) but remaining stable in low responders (n = 9), and more than 50% of top Component 2 RNAs were differentially expressed at day 28.

sources.quote: Among young high responders ( n = 7), Component 2 RNAs decreased in expression on days 7‐28, whereas in low responders ( n = 9) the expression levels remained stable (Figure 6a ).

we performed a DE analysis on the set of top 5% scoring RNAs from Component 2 between young adult high‐ and low responders at each day post‐vaccination, and found that more than 50% of the RNAs were significantly DE on day 28, while there were no significant differences at the other timepoints (Figure 6a ). These genes include PF4 and PPBP and are enriched in pathways associated with platelet response (Figure 6b,c ).
Blood samples were collected prior to vaccination (day 0) and follow‐up days 2, 7, and 28.

claim_4.claim: Flow Cytometry analysis of platelet-rich plasma from a subset of participants at baseline before vaccination (day 0) and days 2 and 7 after vaccination (day 2 and day 7) showed surface expression of CD62p, CD40L, and CD63 was significantly higher in Older (Comm) than in Young adults at all measured days, whereas Older (SNF) had significantly lower expression than Older (Comm) and was generally comparable to Young adults except for higher day 0 CD62p.

sources.quote: The levels of surface expression of all three proteins were significantly increased in platelets from Older (Comm), compared to young adults at day 0, 2, and 7, suggesting an age‐associated increase in platelet activation.

However, surface expression in Older (SNF) adults was significantly decreased compared to Older (Comm), with Older (SNF) activation marker surface expression comparable to that of platelets from young adults (with the exception of Day 0 CD62p expression in Older (SNF) adults, which was significantly higher compared to platelets from young adults) (Figure 5c,f ).
Platelet function was further assessed by flow cytometry at Days 0, 2, and 7 post‐vaccine in a subset of participants where flow cytometry was done immediately after PRP isolation.

claim_5.claim: Flow Cytometry analysis of platelet-rich plasma showed CD62p/SELP protein fold-change at days 2 and 7 after vaccination (day 2 and day 7), normalized to baseline before vaccination (day 0), paralleled SELP RNA fold-change, with the highest increase in Young adults followed by Older (Comm) and then Older (SNF), whereas CD40L and CD63 did not show a similar RNA-protein correspondence.

sources.quote: We found that expression of SELP RNA at day 2 and day 7 post‐vaccine, normalized to day 0, followed the pattern of platelet activation RNA levels identified by tensor decomposition analysis (Figure 4 ), with highest fold‐change in young adults, followed by Older (Comm) and Older (SNF) adults (Figure 5b ). Notably, the surface expression of CD62p/SELP protein at these post‐vaccine time points relative to day 0 closely resembled the RNA expression pattern (Figure 5d ). We did not observe a similar parallel relationship between normalized RNA expression and protein expression for CD40L and CD63 (Figure 5e,f ).
Blood samples were collected prior to vaccination (day 0) and follow‐up days 2, 7, and 28.

claim_6.claim: Hemagglutination Inhibition analysis of serum from 28 young adults, 20 community-dwelling older adults, and 17 skilled nursing facility-resident older adults collected before vaccination (day 0) and 28 days after vaccination (day 28) showed pre-vaccination platelet RNA differences between high and low responders, with 12 RNAs upregulated and 7 downregulated in high responders, including higher THRB, BLZF1, MPIG6B, and CCR1.

sources.quote: Influenza vaccine antibody response was measured using a standard hemagglutination inhibition assay (HAI). To correct for the inverse correlation between pre‐vaccine HAI titer and fold‐increase post‐vaccine, we employed maximum residual after baseline adjustment (maxRBA), a metric which models HAI titer fold changes as an exponential function of strain‐specific baseline titers and selects the maximum residual across strains (Avey et al., 2020 ) (Figure S1 ). maxRBA was used to classify high and low vaccine responders for assessment of platelet transcriptomic differences in vaccine responsiveness.

In order to understand how pre‐vaccination transcriptional state is associated with post‐vaccination antibody response, we performed a DE analysis of high‐ vs. low responders in the pre‐vaccination state, and identified 12 upregulated and 7 down‐regulated RNAs in high responders; upregulated RNAs included THRB, BLZF1, MPIG6B, and CCR1 (Table S7 ).

We enrolled 28 young adults (age 21–35 years), 20 community‐dwelling older adults (age ≥65 years) (Older (Comm)), and 17 older adults (age ≥65 years) (Older (SNF)) who were residents of a skilled nursing facility (SNF) in greater New Haven, Connecticut (Table 1 ).
Antibody response to vaccination was assessed using serum samples obtained at day 0 and 28 using a standard hemagglutination inhibition assay (Frey et al., 2010 ).
